title: Telephone review during spinal cord stimulator trials: costs and consequences of replacing the day 3 clinic visit
subtitle: Economic evaluation (cost-consequence analysis) of a pain service pathway change, 2026 against 2027
statement: The regional pain service runs about 90 spinal cord stimulator trials a year, each with an in-person day 3 visit that changed management for 9 of 88 patients last year. From January 2027 the day 3 visit becomes a structured nurse telephone review with a same-day slot for flagged problems. The service needs to know what the change costs and saves once nurse time, unplanned visits, infections and patient and companion costs are counted, and how certain that answer is.
whoAffected: Adults having a percutaneous spinal cord stimulator trial and the relatives who accompany them, many travelling more than an hour each way; the neuromodulation nurses who will make the calls; the clinic and emergency department services that absorb unplanned visits.
whatHurts: A long round trip on day 3 for a visit that rarely changes management, a companion's lost working day, and the risk that problems such as wound infection are missed or pushed into emergency attendances if the visit is removed without a safety net.
currentPractice: Two in-person visits during the seven-day trial: day 3 for a wound check and programming questions, day 8 for the pain diary review, the permanent implant decision and lead removal.
whyNow: The telephone pathway starts on 2027-01-04, so the year before and the year after can be compared from existing records, and the service manager wants a costed answer before the pathway is extended to implant follow-up.
constraints: No research funding; the evaluation uses existing pain service records and the finance department's unit costs only. The nurse consultant has four protected hours a week for the evaluation from January to December 2027. The telephone pathway is already approved and will not be withheld from any patient.
patientCenteredGoal: Patients get through the trial week safely with fewer journeys, and any problem is still found and treated quickly.
summary: Problem framed as a cost-consequence question about a pathway change, from the health service and patient perspectives.
